messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Amir, a 34‑year‑old South‑Eastern Asian chaplain, has carried the weight of a mugging for almost a year. The night he was robbed, he had stepped off a late‑night train and waited at a dimly lit bus stop. Two men in dark jackets approached, their breaths heavy and metallic. They shoved him against the concrete, demanded his wallet, and then fled into a crowd of commuters. The sight of the shaking figures, the sharp inhale of the attackers, and the hiss of their hurried footsteps etched themselves into Amir’s memory as sharp, almost pictorial images. When he thinks of that night, a cold sweat runs down his back and a stench of gasoline—he had caught a whiff of it as the men drove away—floods his senses. The images come back so vividly that his heart races and a wave of rage surges, as if the attackers were still there. The moment Amir enters a crowded street, hears someone’s heavy breathing, or sees a person who resembles one of the assailants, his mind flips back to that bus stop. The presence of people related to the event, the thronging crowds, and the sound of deep, uneven breaths become triggers that ignite his memories. Each trigger pulls Amir’s mind into that night, and the vivid pictures, scents, and rage flood his consciousness. In those flashes he feels a sudden, overwhelming sense of helplessness, as though he had been powerless to protect himself. The terror of that memory fuels a belief that he must be weak—he blames his own character, convinced that the mugging happened to him because of who he is, that his life’s circumstances made him a target. These negative appraisals feed back into the memory loop: the more he ruminates on the image of the attack, the stronger his conviction that he is destined to be victimized, and the more the memory itself becomes more vivid and terrifying. As Amir’s mind wrestles with these loops, the negative appraisals also color his view of other people. He compares himself with those who had avoided the bus stop or who had not been robbed; he feels that they were somehow better or luckier. This self‑comparison sharpens his sense of isolation and amplifies the memory’s intensity. In turn, the intense memory of the mugging and the negative appraisal that it happened to him because of his “character” pushes him to shun any situation that could trigger the flashback. He has stopped walking near bus stops, he no longer attends large community gatherings, and he avoids the church’s busy Sunday services, where crowds of parishioners fill the nave. Each avoidance step feels necessary, a protective barrier against the possibility of a repetition. Yet the very avoidance he believes will keep him safe also leaves him feeling disconnected from the pastoral community he loves and undermines his ability to minister effectively. During the last few months, Amir’s avoidance has cost him a promotion at the hospice he serves. He declined the offer to lead the weekly counseling group because the venue is a packed auditorium and the rush of voices and footsteps reminds him too starkly of that night. He also declined a weekend retreat that would have brought him closer to his faith community, because the packed church hall triggers the memory of the attacker’s heavy breaths. Each of these professional setbacks feeds back into his sense of helplessness; he feels that he cannot control his own life and that his career is being derailed because of a single event. He has come to believe that his future is a series of unavoidable, negative events, and the fear of another encounter keeps him in a perpetual state of hyper‑vigilance. Amir finally came to the clinic when the memory‑triggered rage escalated into a night where he could not sleep, and the days when he could not leave his apartment without a plan to flee. He worries that one moment could bring the attacker back into his life, that the heavy breathing will again signal imminent danger. What terrifies him most is the feeling that he is stuck in a cycle he cannot break, that his thoughts of the mugging keep him trapped in a state of fear and anger, and that his identity as a chaplain—someone who is supposed to provide solace—is at odds with the relentless terror that consumes him. He hopes for a way to quiet the images, to stop the shameful feeling that the attack was his fault, and to find the courage to step back into the world he once loved.
